conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: TightTradingRangeWidthTest
candidates.quote: If the average daily range in the Emini has been about 10 to 15 points, then any trading range that is three points tall or smaller is probably a tight trading range.
candidates.description: A tight trading range is a horizontal range whose height (highest high to lowest low over the last N bars) is small relative to the recent average daily range -- a size-based proxy that is more directly mechanizable than pure bar-overlap counting.

complexity.reason: a window loop for the highest/lowest of the range plus an average of daily ranges; no pivot detection needed

notes: This is the explicit ATR/ADR-sized proxy the task asked for, as an alternative mechanization to R00-21 (TightTradingRange, front matter), which instead counts bar-overlap. tightRangeFraction = 0.24 is a reading of the book's '3 of 10-15 points' example; expect the dedup pass to reconcile with R00-21.
Brooks also allows a taller range (4-5 points) to still count as tight 'if the bars are large' -- not modeled here; see notes on R22-14 for the bar-size angle.

candidates.name: SlopingTightChannelWidthTest
candidates.quote: When a tight trading range slopes slightly up or down, it is still a tight trading range and it should be treated the same way... This is the same for a tight channel, which is just a sloping tight trading range.
candidates.description: Generalizes R22-01 to a sloped micro-channel: the perpendicular width between the fitted upper and lower channel lines over the lookback window is small relative to the average daily range.

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and trend-channel-line projection (trends chapter 14) in addition to R22-01's size test

candidates.name: BarbwirePattern
candidates.quote: If you see three or more bars that largely overlap and one or more of them has a tiny body (doji), this is barbwire. As a guide for how much overlap is enough, look at the second of the three bars... If more than half of its height is within the range of the bars before and after it, you should view the three bars as barbwire.
candidates.description: Shared primitive for this chapter: barbwire is three or more consecutive largely-overlapping bars where at least one is a doji and the middle bar's range is more than half contained within the range spanned by its two neighbors.

complexity.reason: a fixed three-bar overlap-containment test plus a doji test on each of the three bars

notes: A special case of a tight trading range (R22-01/R00-21) named by Brooks; often forms next to the moving average.
Doji primitive presumably already defined in trends chapter 2 (Trend Bars, Doji Bars, and Climaxes); reused here rather than redefined.

candidates.name: TightTradingRangeBlocksAllEntriesSwitch
candidates.quote: A tight trading range trumps everything, and that especially means all of the great reasons for taking any trade. It does not matter what else you see on the chart... Once you see that the market is in a tight trading range, don't trade.
candidates.description: While the market is in a tight trading range, block all new entries regardless of any other signal that would otherwise fire -- the single global override this chapter argues for most strongly.

complexity.reason: a direct pass-through of the tight-trading-range regime flag into a global block, once that flag exists

notes: This is the chapter's central, most distinctive and most literally-stated rule -- explicitly phrased as overriding every other setup -- and maps directly onto the engine's Switch role.
Depends on whichever tight-trading-range detector the dedup pass keeps (R22-01, R22-03 BarbwirePattern, or R00-21).

candidates.name: ExitToBreakevenWhenPositionEntersTightRange
candidates.quote: If they just entered a position and the pattern grows into a tight trading range, the best option is to try to get out at breakeven or maybe with a tick loss, and then wait for the breakout before deciding on your next trade.
candidates.description: If a trade was entered before the market was recognized as a tight trading range, and the pattern has since formed, exit at breakeven (or a small loss) rather than holding for the original target.
candidates.pseudocode: exitLong = isTightTradingRange[0] && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() <= breakevenTolerance && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() >= -breakevenTolerance - smallLossAllowance;
candidates.book_order_type: market or limit exit near the entry price

complexity.reason: combines the tight-trading-range regime detector with an open-profit-near-zero test

notes: As written this only fires near breakeven; the book's fallback (hold with a wide stop) is explicitly called 'less sound' and not mechanized here (see R22-08 for a time-based alternative).

candidates.name: FailedBreakoutCountIncreasesNextBreakoutOddsFilter
candidates.quote: After two failed breakouts, the odds were much higher that a third breakout would succeed.
candidates.description: Within a tight trading range, count failed breakout attempts on one side; once the count reaches a threshold, permit (or upweight) a with-direction breakout entry on the next attempt.

complexity.reason: needs a failed-breakout-attempt counter, which itself needs a bar-level definition of 'failed', composed with the tight-trading-range regime

candidates.name: PreferWithTrendBreakoutAfterTightRangeFilter
candidates.quote: if a tight trading range forms after a trend leg, the probability that the breakout will be in the direction of the trend can be as high as 55 percent if the trend was strong... the odds still ultimately favor a with-trend breakout.
candidates.description: When a tight trading range forms after a trend leg (and was not preceded by a climactic reversal), only take breakout entries in the direction of the prior always-in trend; treat countertrend breakouts as low-probability.

complexity.reason: reuses the existing AlwaysInDirection primitive as the trend reference; the 'preceded by a climactic reversal' exception is not modeled

notes: The exception -- 'if it forms after a climactic reversal, even a small one, the market has an equal probability of breaking out in either direction' -- would need a climax detector to model and is left out here; a candidate for a future climax-detection chapter.

candidates.name: ExitWithTrendEntryIfRangeFailsToExpand
candidates.quote: If a trader enters with the trend in a tight trading range, expecting the trend to resume, but the market breaks out in the wrong direction, it is usually better to exit and wait for a larger trading range to develop... using a wide stop and holding for a long time is usually not a good strategy.
candidates.description: If a with-trend entry was taken while the market was a tight trading range, and after N bars the range has neither broken out with-trend nor reached a profit target, exit rather than hold through a wide stop waiting for the range to expand.

complexity.reason: a bar-count-since-entry time stop gated by the tight-trading-range regime and a non-positive open-profit test

notes: Same shape as the catalog's NumBarsIfLosing but additionally gated on the tight-trading-range regime; kept separate because Brooks's rationale (avoid a wide stop while waiting for range expansion) is specific to this context.

candidates.name: BarbwireBreakoutFadeEntry
candidates.quote: The cardinal rule for trading in barbwire is to never enter on a breakout. Instead, wait for a trend bar to break out of the pattern... as soon as the bull trend bar closes, place an order to go short at one tick below the low of that breakout bar... Do not fade the breakout if it has two or more consecutive trend bars.
candidates.description: When a single trend bar breaks out of a barbwire pattern (not two or more consecutive trend bars in the same direction), fade it: enter opposite the breakout one tick beyond the breakout bar's far side.
candidates.pseudocode:
isSingleBarBreakout = isBarbwire[1] && isBullTrendBar(open[0], high[0], low[0], close[0], bodyFraction) && !isBullTrendBar(open[1], high[1], low[1], close[1], bodyFraction);
enterShortNextBarOpen = isSingleBarBreakout && low[0] > barbwireHigh[1]; // breakout closed above the pattern; fade with a sell stop one tick below low[0]
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop one tick below the low of the single breakout trend bar

complexity.reason: composes the barbwire primitive with a trend-bar test and a consecutive-bar-count gate

notes: Brooks says this fade itself frequently fails, and the failure is a high-probability second entry back in the breakout direction -- see R22-10.

candidates.name: BarbwireFadeFailureReversalEntry
candidates.quote: Sometimes this short entry will fail, so once short and once the entry bar closes, place an order to reverse to long at one tick above the high of the short entry bar, which would become a breakout pullback buy entry. It is unusual for the second entry to fail.
candidates.description: If the barbwire breakout fade (R22-09) is entered and its own entry bar closes against the fade (i.e., the fade is failing), reverse to a breakout-pullback entry one tick beyond the fade entry bar's far side, in the original breakout direction.
candidates.pseudocode:
fadeEntryBarFailed = ctx.MarketPosition() < 0 && close[0] > open[0]; // short fade entry bar closed back up
enterLongNextBarOpen = fadeEntryBarFailed; // buy stop one tick above high[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the high of the (failed) fade entry bar

complexity.reason: reads position state and the immediately preceding fade entry's outcome; the arithmetic itself is a simple next-bar stop

notes: Reads position state deliberately, like the catalog's FlatOrOpenLossExceeds -- it decides whether a fresh signal should reverse the open fade trade.

candidates.name: TradingRangeMajoritySideOfEmaFilter
candidates.quote: One very good rule is that if there is a trading range setting up and it is near the moving average, never look to buy if the bars are mostly below the moving average, and never look to sell if the bars are mostly above the moving average... when barbwire forms adjacent to the moving average, it will usually break out in the direction away from the moving average.
candidates.description: While a trading range/barbwire is forming near the 20-bar EMA, only allow entries in the direction implied by which side of the EMA most of the pattern's bars sit on: block longs when most bars are below the EMA, block shorts when most are above it.

complexity.reason: an EMA plus a bar-majority count over the pattern window

notes: Brooks states this twice in the chapter (once generally, once specifically for barbwire adjacent to the EMA); one candidate covers both statements.

candidates.name: BarbwireSmallBarFadeAtExtreme
candidates.quote: You can also fade small bars near the top and bottom of barbwire if there is an entry. For example, if there is a small bar near the high, especially if it is a bear reversal bar, look to scalp a short with an entry order to sell at one tick below the low of that bar on a stop.
candidates.description: Within barbwire, fade a small bar (range well below the pattern's typical bar size) that forms near the top of the pattern by shorting one tick below its low (mirrored: buy above a small bar near the bottom).
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop one tick below the low of the small bar

complexity.reason: a relative bar-size test plus a range-extreme location test, gated on the barbwire primitive

candidates.name: AvoidFading1MinuteBarsFilter
candidates.quote: You should rarely, if ever, fade off 1 minute bars, because the 3 and 5 minute bars provide better winning percentages.
candidates.description: Do not take fade (countertrend scalp) entries when the chart's bar interval is 1 minute; prefer 3-minute or 5-minute bars for these setups.

complexity.reason: a constant comparison against the chart's configured bar interval

candidates.name: BarbwireBarSizeAboveAverageFilter
candidates.quote: A range of four and sometimes five points can sometimes behave like a tight trading range as well if the bars are large... it is more effective if the bars are at least as large as the average bars of the day. If the bars are too small and the range is too tight, then the odds of a successful scalp are less.
candidates.description: Only take barbwire/tight-range scalp entries when the individual bars are at least as large as the day's average bar range so far; skip setups where both the range and the bars themselves are too small.
candidates.pseudocode:
sessionAvgBarRange = average(high - low, barsSinceSessionOpen);
allowScalpEntry = (high[0] - low[0]) >= sessionAvgBarRange;

complexity.reason: needs a session-relative running average of bar range, same as R21-13

notes: Same session-average-bar-range measure as R21-13 (SessionAverageBarRangeMoneyStop, chapter 21); likely mergeable into one shared primitive.

candidates.name: ThreeConsecutiveSellClimaxesPredictCorrectionFilter
candidates.quote: This was the third consecutive sell climax of the day... After three consecutive sell climaxes, the market usually corrects sideways to up for at least 10 bars and with at least two legs.
candidates.description: After three consecutive sell (buy) climaxes within a session, favor long (short) entries and disfavor further with-trend short (long) entries, expecting a multi-bar, two-legged correction.

complexity.reason: needs a climax/spike classifier and a counter that persists and resets across a session

candidates.name: ReverseOnOppositeSignalInTightRangeWithRoom
candidates.quote: If you bought in a tight trading range in a bear trend and the market formed a low 2, you should exit and possibly reverse to short. If you shorted in that bear tight trading range and the market then formed a high 2, you should exit and possibly reverse to long, but only if the signal bar is a bull bar at the bottom of the range and there is enough room to the top of the pattern for a scalper's profit.
candidates.description: While long in a tight trading range, an opposite (Low 2) signal is grounds to exit and reverse to short; while short, an opposite (High 2) signal with a favorable signal bar is grounds to reverse to long, but only if there is enough remaining room within the range to reach a scalper's profit target.
candidates.pseudocode:
hasRoomToTarget = (rangeHigh[0] - close[0]) >= minScalpTicks * tickSize; // room from here to the top of the range for a long reversal
enterLongNextBarOpen = ctx.MarketPosition() < 0 && isTightTradingRange[0] && isHigh2Setup[0] && isBullSignalBar[0] && hasRoomToTarget;
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop above the High 2 signal bar, closing the short and opening long

complexity.reason: reads position state (like FlatOrOpenLossExceeds) and composes the High2/Low2 pattern with a room-to-target measurement inside the tight-range regime

notes: Brooks flags this as rarely a good trade, only for very experienced traders -- recorded as stated, not endorsed.

candidates.name: BarbwireAfterFirstHourSpikeMarksExtremeOfDayFilter
candidates.quote: Sometimes barbwire forms at the end of a several-bar spike in the first hour. When it happens in an area of support in a bull trend, it can become a reversal pattern and the low of the day. When this happens after a bull spike in the first hour at an area of resistance, it can become the high of the day.
candidates.description: Barbwire that forms at the end of a multi-bar spike within the first hour of the session, at a support or resistance area, is a candidate reversal pattern for the low (or high) of the day.
candidates.pseudocode:
// research: 'area of support/resistance' needs a design decision (e.g., prior swing level or moving average)
isCandidateDayExtreme = isBarbwire[0] && barsSinceSessionOpen <= firstHourBars && endsMultiBarSpike[0] && nearSupportOrResistance[0];
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context classification feeding a reversal entry defined elsewhere)

complexity.reason: 'area of support/resistance' and 'ends a multi-bar spike' are not given precise bar-level tests in this passage

notes: firstHourBars=12 assumes 5-minute bars, same convention as R21-14.

rejected.quote: Although no one knows what algorithms are being used by the quants at high-frequency trading (HFT) firms, the huge volume taking place and the small moves with lots of reversals could easily be the result of programs trying to scalp one to four ticks repeatedly.
rejected.reason: requires knowledge of other market participants' order flow/algorithms, not available from OHLCV bars

rejected.quote: The first idea that they consider is a martingale approach where they double or triple the size of their next trade after each loss... Anyone blindly doubling up after consecutive losers is gambling and not trading.
rejected.reason: a position-sizing/money-management scheme, not a bar-level entry or exit test; the engine's single-clip Entry/Exit/Switch model has no variable position-size mechanism to hang this on

rejected.quote: Fibonacci traders would call the rally to bar 10 a 61.8 percent pullback and say that it was close enough, but every pullback is close enough to some Fibonacci number, making the Fibonacci numbers essentially meaningless most of the time.
rejected.reason: Brooks explicitly dismisses Fibonacci retracement levels as a tautological, non-discriminating filter

rejected.quote: there are always great-looking ones as they are setting up, you have to factor in the probability, which is 50 percent for an equidistant move
rejected.reason: requires a subjective probability-of-success estimate, not a value decidable from OHLCV bars (same family as the R21 rejection)

chapter_summary: Chapter 22 defines the tight trading range and its emotionally loaded special case, barbwire (three-plus heavily overlapping bars with at least one doji), and argues at length that both should mostly be avoided or, if traded, only faded on single-bar breakouts and re-entered with the breakout on the fade's failure. The most mechanizable material is exactly the kind the task asked for: an ATR/average-daily-range-sized width test for 'tight' (R22-01, generalized to sloped channels in R22-02), the barbwire bar-overlap-plus-doji primitive (R22-03), and a direct Switch candidate (R22-04) mechanizing Brooks's literal claim that a tight trading range 'trumps everything' and should block all entries. Also produced: majority-side-of-EMA and bar-size/bar-interval quality filters, failed-breakout-count and consecutive-sell-climax context filters (both research/hard, needing counters this chapter does not itself define), and several composite fade/reversal entries built on the barbwire primitive. Four items were rejected: HFT order-flow speculation, martingale position sizing, Brooks's own dismissal of Fibonacci levels, and a bare 50-percent equidistant-move probability claim.
